title: Why the British love queues
text: If you visit Britain, you will soon notice something: people stand in neat lines almost everywhere. They queue at bus stops, in shops, at the post office and even outside popular cafes. In the United States people usually say 'line', but in Britain the word is 'queue', and the habit is a famous part of daily life. The idea behind it is fairness. The person who arrived first should be served first. Jumping the queue, which means pushing in front of other people, is considered very rude, and a British person may show their annoyance with a loud sigh or a polite cough instead of an angry shout. Historians often link the habit to the twentieth century. During and after the Second World War, food and other goods were rationed, so shoppers waited in long lines, and a calm, orderly way of waiting became normal. Rationing in Britain did not completely end until 1954. The humorous writer George Mikes, who moved to London from Hungary, joked that an Englishman who is alone will still form an orderly queue of one. The joke works because the habit is so well known. Today queueing is still a social rule. At the Wimbledon tennis tournament, fans wait in a long line, called simply 'the Queue', for tickets on the day, and many bring tents, snacks and folding chairs. So if you go to Britain, remember the simple advice: find the end of the line and wait your turn.

What do many British people do if someone jumps the queue?
options: Show annoyance politely, for example with a sigh

questions.q: What do some fans do at Wimbledon?
options: Wait in a long queue for tickets, sometimes with tents
Buy all their tickets by post
Watch the matches from the street only

title: Pancake Day in the UK
text: Every year, usually in February or March, British families make pancakes on a day with two names: Shrove Tuesday and Pancake Day. It falls the day before Ash Wednesday, and the date changes each year because it depends on the date of Easter. In the past, people used up rich foods such as eggs, milk and butter before a long period of simple eating. Pancakes were an easy way to use these ingredients, and the tradition has continued for hundreds of years even though most families now simply enjoy the food. British pancakes are thin, a bit like French crepes, and are very different from the thick American ones. A classic way to eat them is with lemon juice and sugar. Others prefer chocolate spread, jam, syrup or fruit. Making them also includes a bit of fun: many people try to toss the pancake in the frying pan and catch it as it flips over. When it works, everyone cheers. When it lands on the floor, everyone laughs. Some towns hold pancake races. In the town of Olney, in Buckinghamshire, women run through the streets while carrying a frying pan with a pancake in it, and they must toss it at the start and again at the finish. This race is said to have been run since the fifteenth century. Schools and charities around the country copy the idea, so you may see runners in aprons and chef hats on the high street.

questions.q: What is another name for Pancake Day?
How do British pancakes usually differ from American ones?
options: They are always sweet and round

questions.q: What happens in the pancake race at Olney?
options: Runners bake pancakes in an oven
Runners carry a frying pan and toss a pancake
Runners eat pancakes on a stage

title: Thanksgiving in the United States
text: Thanksgiving is one of the biggest family holidays in the United States. It takes place on the fourth Thursday of November, and many people travel long distances to be with relatives. It is a time to say thank you for the good things in life, and above all it is a time to eat together. The traditional meal centres on a roast turkey. Around it you will usually find mashed potatoes, gravy, stuffing, cranberry sauce, corn and sweet potatoes. For dessert, the most typical choice is pumpkin pie. Families often argue happily about whose recipe is best, and nearly everyone ends the day feeling very full. The story people often tell goes back to 1621, when settlers from England, known as the Pilgrims, shared an autumn harvest meal with members of the Wampanoag people in what is now Massachusetts. Historians say this was one of several harvest celebrations in early America, and the modern holiday grew slowly from many such traditions. President Abraham Lincoln declared a national day of thanksgiving in 1863, and in 1941 Congress made the fourth Thursday of November an official holiday. Other traditions have become part of the day. Many people watch the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City, which has giant balloons of cartoon characters. Others watch American football on television. The day after, called Black Friday, is the start of the Christmas shopping season. Canada has its own Thanksgiving, but it is held in October.

questions.q: When is Thanksgiving in the United States?
options: On the fourth Thursday of November
On the first Monday of October
On the last day of December

title: Machu Picchu: the city in the clouds
text: High in the Andes of Peru, about 2,430 metres above sea level, stands one of the most famous places in the world: Machu Picchu. The name comes from Quechua and is often translated as 'old mountain'. The site sits on a ridge above the Urubamba River, and on many mornings clouds drift between the stone buildings and the green peaks around them. Machu Picchu was built in the fifteenth century, probably as a royal estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The Incas were expert builders. Many walls are made of carefully cut stones that fit together so tightly that you cannot slide a knife blade between them, and they used no mortar. The terraces on the hillsides helped to grow crops and also protected the slopes from landslides. The Spanish conquerors never found the city, which is one reason it survived in such good condition. Local families knew about it, but it became famous around the world in 1911, when the American explorer Hiram Bingham, guided by local people, brought it to international attention. In 1983 UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site, and in 2007 it was chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Today many visitors arrive by train from Cusco or walk the Inca Trail, a path of about 43 kilometres that takes four days. To protect the site, the number of visitors per day is limited, and tickets must be booked in advance.

questions.q: What does the name Machu Picchu come from?
Why did the city survive in good condition?
options: It was rebuilt in the twentieth century
It was always full of visitors
The Spanish conquerors never found it

questions.q: What is the Inca Trail?
options: A path to Machu Picchu of about 43 kilometres

title: The kiwi: a bird that cannot fly
text: New Zealand is home to many unusual animals, but the kiwi is the most famous. It is a small brown bird about the size of a chicken, with a long thin beak and tiny wings that you can hardly see under its shaggy feathers. It cannot fly at all. Because the bird is so well known, New Zealanders are often called 'Kiwis' around the world, and the word is not only about the fruit. Kiwi live in forests and grasslands. They sleep during the day in burrows and come out at night to look for food. Their nostrils are at the end of the beak, which is unusual for a bird, so they can smell worms and insects under the ground. They push the beak into the soil and sniff, a bit like a tiny vacuum cleaner. The kiwi also lays one of the biggest eggs compared with the size of the bird. The egg can be about a fifth of the mother's weight. In many kinds of kiwi, the father sits on the egg for weeks until it hatches. Sadly, there are fewer kiwi than before. Before humans arrived, New Zealand had almost no land mammals, so ground birds lived without many dangers. Then people brought animals such as stoats, cats and dogs, which hunt kiwi and their chicks. Today volunteers and scientists set traps, protect nesting areas and run special sanctuaries to help the birds survive.

questions.q: Why can the kiwi smell food under the ground?
options: Its nostrils are at the end of its beak

questions.q: When are kiwi most active?
Why are kiwi in danger?
options: There is no food in New Zealand
Animals brought by people hunt them
They fly away to other countries

title: Surfing at Chicama, the world's longest wave
text: On the north coast of Peru, near the small port of Puerto Malabrigo in the La Libertad region, there is a place that surfers dream about: Chicama. It is often described as the longest left-hand wave in the world. Surfers say that on a perfect day a single ride can last for more than a kilometre, and some people claim that it can reach about two kilometres. The wave is so long because of the shape of the coast and the sea floor. Swells from the Pacific Ocean reach a long, gently curving bay, and the wave breaks slowly along it instead of all at once. This gives surfers a very long ride and plenty of time to turn and enjoy the view. The best swells usually arrive between April and October, during the southern autumn and winter. Surfing has a very long history in Peru. For centuries fishermen used small boats made of totora reeds, called caballitos de totora, to ride waves near the coast. Many people see these boats as an ancient ancestor of modern surfing, and you can still see them today at beaches such as Huanchaco, near Trujillo. Peru has also produced world champions. Sofia Mulanovich from Punta Hermosa won the women's world surfing title in 2004, which made her the first South American to win a world title. Her success helped young Peruvians to see surfing as a serious sport.

questions.q: Why is the wave at Chicama so long?
options: The coast and sea floor make it break slowly along a bay
It is made by a machine

questions.q: What are caballitos de totora?
options: A kind of surfboard made of plastic

title: The potato: a gift from Peru
text: The potato is one of the most popular foods on the planet, and its story begins in the Andes. Farmers near Lake Titicaca, in what is now Peru and Bolivia, began to grow potatoes thousands of years ago, perhaps around 8,000 years ago. Today Peru grows thousands of different kinds, in colours such as yellow, purple, red and nearly black, and many shapes too. Why was it so important? A potato grows well in cold, high places where other crops struggle, and it gives plenty of energy. The Incas also invented a clever way to keep potatoes for years. They left them outside to freeze at night and dry in the sun by day, then pressed them to remove the water. The result is called chuno, and it can be stored for a very long time. Spanish sailors took potatoes to Europe in the sixteenth century. At first many Europeans did not trust them, because the plant is related to poisonous plants. Slowly, though, farmers saw that potatoes fed families well, and the crop became very important in places such as Ireland, Germany and Russia. Later the potato travelled to every continent. Today it is the fourth most important food crop in the world, after rice, wheat and maize. In 2008 the United Nations celebrated the International Year of the Potato. Peru also has a National Potato Day, celebrated on 30 May. Peruvian dishes such as papa a la huancaina and causa show how proud the country is of its most famous vegetable.

questions.q: Where did potato farming begin?
What is chuno?
options: A kind of soup from Lima
Potatoes frozen and dried to be stored for a long time

questions.q: How did potatoes reach Europe?
options: Spanish sailors took them in the sixteenth century

title: Afternoon tea: a very British pause
text: Afternoon tea is a small meal enjoyed in Britain, usually between three and five o'clock. It includes a pot of tea, tiny sandwiches, scones with jam and cream, and little cakes. Many hotels in London serve it on pretty plates with three levels, and people often book a table weeks before. The custom is usually linked to Anna, the Duchess of Bedford, in the 1840s. At that time people ate a big breakfast and a late dinner, around eight o'clock in the evening. The duchess felt hungry in the afternoon, so she asked for tea and snacks in her room. She later invited friends to join her, and the idea became fashionable among wealthy families before spreading to other groups. Tea itself is not grown in Britain. It arrived from China in the seventeenth century, and later large plantations in India and Sri Lanka supplied most of it. Today many British people drink their tea with a splash of milk. Sugar is a matter of taste. A scone is the star of the table, and it has started a friendly argument. In Devon, people put the cream on the scone first and the jam on top. In Cornwall, they do the opposite. Each county is sure that its own way is correct, and neither will change. Whatever you choose, remember that afternoon tea is not a quick lunch. It is a chance to sit down, chat slowly and forget the rush of the day.

questions.q: Who is usually linked with the start of afternoon tea?
Where did tea first come to Britain from?
What is the friendly argument about scones?
options: Whether to eat them hot or cold
Whether the jam or the cream goes first

title: Cricket and the Ashes
text: Cricket is a bat-and-ball game that began in England, where people have played it since at least the sixteenth century. Today it is hugely popular in India, Pakistan, Australia, South Africa, the West Indies and many other countries. Two teams of eleven players take turns to bat and to bowl. The bowler throws the ball towards a set of wooden sticks called the wicket, and the batter tries to hit it away and score runs. Some matches are very short, but a Test match can last up to five days. Players wear white clothes, and there is a tea break in the afternoon. It is perhaps the only sport in which a big game can finish without a winner after five days of play, which is called a draw. The most famous series is the Ashes, played between England and Australia. It began in 1882, when Australia beat England at The Oval in London for the first time on English soil. A newspaper joked that English cricket had died and that its body would be burned and taken to Australia. Soon after, an England captain went to Australia to 'bring back the ashes'. Afterwards a small urn, said to contain the ashes of a burnt wooden bail, was given to him. That tiny urn is kept at Lord's Cricket Ground in London, and the real trophy never travels, although a copy is held up at the end of each series. The two countries still play for the Ashes every few years, and fans on both sides enjoy teasing each other.

title: Big Ben is not a clock
text: Many visitors to London take a photo of Big Ben, but there is a small secret: 'Big Ben' is not the name of the clock or even of the tower. It is the nickname of the huge bell inside. The clock tower at the Palace of Westminster was officially called the Clock Tower until 2012, when it was renamed the Elizabeth Tower to honour Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee. The clock started working in 1859 and has been loved ever since. The tower is about 96 metres tall, and its four clock faces are each about seven metres wide. The main bell weighs around 13.7 tonnes, which is more than two large elephants. Four smaller bells ring the quarter hours. Nobody is completely sure why the bell is called Big Ben. One popular story says the name comes from Sir Benjamin Hall, a politician who was in charge of the work and was a rather large man. Another story suggests it was named after a famous boxer of the time, Benjamin Caunt. Both stories are told today, and neither can be proved. The clock is known for being very accurate, and workers have sometimes kept the time correct by putting old pennies on the pendulum. A single penny changes the speed by a small fraction of a second each day. Between 2017 and 2022, the tower was repaired and its bells fell silent for most of that time. They returned in 2022 to the delight of Londoners.

questions.q: What is 'Big Ben' really?
options: The name of the whole palace
The nickname of the great bell
The name of the River Thames

questions.q: When was the tower renamed the Elizabeth Tower?
How have workers adjusted the clock's time?
options: By adding old pennies to the pendulum
By turning the hands by hand every hour

title: Halloween and the story of the jack-o'-lantern
text: On 31 October, children in many countries dress up as witches, ghosts and cartoon heroes, knock on doors and shout 'Trick or treat!'. Halloween is now especially big in the United States, but its roots lie in Ireland and Scotland. Long ago, the ancient Celts celebrated a festival called Samhain, which marked the end of the harvest and the start of the dark winter. People believed that on that night the border between the living world and the world of spirits became thin. To avoid trouble, they lit bonfires and wore costumes so that spirits would not recognise them. Carved lanterns are another old tradition. In Ireland and Scotland people carved faces into turnips, and put a candle inside to keep away spooky visitors. The name 'jack-o'-lantern' comes from an Irish folk tale about a man called Stingy Jack, who played tricks and was left to wander in the dark with only a glowing coal in a turnip. In the nineteenth century, many Irish families emigrated to America. There they found that pumpkins were bigger, softer and easier to carve, so the pumpkin lantern replaced the turnip. The custom of going from door to door became popular in North America in the twentieth century. Today people spend billions of dollars on sweets and costumes every year. In Peru, 31 October is also the Day of Criollo Music, so some families celebrate both.

questions.q: What was Samhain?
options: An old Celtic festival at the end of the harvest

questions.q: What did people first carve for lanterns?
Why did the pumpkin replace the turnip in America?
options: Turnips were not available at all
Pumpkins were bigger and easier to carve

title: Kangaroos: hoppers of Australia
text: The kangaroo is a symbol of Australia, and it appears on coins, airplanes and sports shirts. Kangaroos are marsupials, which means that mothers carry their babies in a pouch. Australia has more than fifty kinds of kangaroo and their close relatives, such as wallabies, and experts believe there are more kangaroos than people in the country. The biggest one is the red kangaroo. A male can stand almost two metres tall and weigh up to ninety kilograms. Kangaroos move by hopping, and they use their strong back legs and their long tail for balance. A hopping kangaroo can reach about sixty kilometres an hour for short distances, and it can leap several metres in a single jump. The way they hop saves energy, which helps them live in dry parts of the continent. A baby kangaroo is called a joey. When it is born, it is only about as big as a jelly bean. It crawls up the mother's fur and climbs into the pouch, where it drinks milk and grows. After several months it starts to look out, and later it leaves the pouch to eat grass, but it may still return when it feels scared. Kangaroos can swim well, and they cannot easily walk backwards. Some people think this is why the animal is on the national coat of arms, next to the emu, as a sign of a country always moving forward. Drivers in the countryside see road signs warning them that kangaroos may cross.

questions.q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
How do kangaroos move quickly?
What is the kangaroo's pouch for?
options: Keeping the animal warm in the rain

title: Inti Raymi: the Festival of the Sun
text: Every year on 24 June, thousands of people gather in the Peruvian city of Cusco to watch Inti Raymi, which means 'Festival of the Sun' in Quechua. In the southern hemisphere, the winter solstice happens around 21 June, the shortest day of the year. For the Incas, the sun god Inti was extremely important, so they held a great ceremony to ask him to return and bring warmth and good harvests. In Inca times the emperor led the festival, with music, dances, processions and offerings. After the Spanish took control of the region, the celebration was banned in 1572 because the authorities did not approve of it. For almost four hundred years it was not held in its original form. In 1944 a Cusco scholar and artist, Faustino Espinoza Navarro, helped to bring it back as a theatrical recreation based on historical accounts. Since then it has been staged each year. An actor plays the Sapa Inca, the emperor, and hundreds of performers wear bright costumes, with feathers, gold-coloured ornaments and woven cloth. The show moves through three places. It begins at the Qorikancha, an Inca temple in the centre of Cusco, continues to the Plaza de Armas and ends in the huge stone fields of Sacsayhuaman, above the city. The festival is performed in Quechua, so many visitors read a programme in English or Spanish to follow the story. It is now one of the biggest festivals in South America, and it is the highlight of the Cusco tourist season.

title: Baseball: America's pastime
text: Baseball is often called America's pastime. Two teams of nine players take turns. One team bats, and the other plays in the field. The pitcher throws a small hard ball, and the batter tries to hit it and run around four bases to score. A game normally has nine innings, and the team with more runs at the end wins. You may have heard that Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown in 1839. In fact, historians say this story is a myth. The game grew from older bat-and-ball games played in England and America, such as rounders. An important early step was in 1845, when a New York team called the Knickerbockers wrote a set of rules, which are often credited to Alexander Cartwright. Professional baseball started in the nineteenth century, and today the biggest competition is Major League Baseball, which ends every October with the World Series. Many fans bring their gloves to games hoping to catch a ball that flies into the crowd. Hot dogs, peanuts and popcorn are classic snacks. In the middle of the seventh inning, everyone stands up and sings 'Take Me Out to the Ball Game', a song written in 1908. This moment is called the seventh-inning stretch. Baseball is also very popular in Japan, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela and Mexico. Many of the best players in the American leagues come from these countries.

What do historians say about the Doubleday story?
options: It was proven by a film

questions.q: What song do fans sing in the seventh inning?
options: Take Me Out to the Ball Game

title: The Great Barrier Reef
text: Off the north-east coast of Australia lies the biggest coral reef system on Earth: the Great Barrier Reef. It stretches for about 2,300 kilometres, which is roughly the distance between London and Moscow, and it is made of more than 2,900 separate reefs and around 900 islands. It is so large that astronauts can see it from space. A coral reef is built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Many people think coral is a plant or a rock, but it is a living animal that makes a hard skeleton. Over thousands of years, billions of these skeletons have formed the reef. Inside the coral's tissue live microscopic algae that give it colour and food. The reef is home to an incredible variety of life. Scientists have recorded around 1,500 species of fish, thousands of kinds of mollusc, six species of sea turtle and many types of whale and dolphin. Divers can swim with colourful clownfish, giant clams and graceful manta rays. UNESCO made the reef a World Heritage Site in 1981. However, the reef is under pressure. When the sea becomes too warm, corals push out their algae and turn white. This is called coral bleaching, and if the warm water lasts too long, the coral can die. Scientists and local workers are testing ways to protect it, such as planting new coral and monitoring water quality. Tourists who visit are asked to use sunscreen that is safe for the reef and never to touch the coral.

questions.q: What builds the Great Barrier Reef?
What is coral bleaching?
options: Corals turning white when the sea is too warm

title: Maple syrup: Canada's sweet treasure
text: Canada produces most of the world's maple syrup, usually about three quarters of the total, and the majority of it comes from the province of Quebec. The maple leaf is also the symbol on the Canadian flag, which has had this design since 1965. Syrup starts as sap, a clear liquid inside the maple tree. The sap is almost like water with a tiny bit of sugar. To make syrup, workers boil it for hours until most of the water has evaporated. It takes around forty litres of sap to produce just one litre of syrup, which explains why real maple syrup is not cheap. The timing is important. Sap runs best in late winter and early spring, when the nights are below freezing and the days are warmer. In March, farmers drill small holes in the trunks and collect the sap in buckets or through plastic tubes. Indigenous peoples of North America were the first to make maple syrup, and they taught the method to the European settlers. Canadians use syrup in many ways. They pour it over pancakes, of course, but also add it to baked beans, salmon and ice cream. A favourite spring treat is maple taffy, in which hot syrup is poured onto clean snow, where it cools into a sticky toffee that you roll onto a wooden stick. Many families visit a 'sugar shack', a small farm building where syrup is made, to eat a big meal and enjoy the first signs of spring.

When does sap run best?
options: In the hottest part of summer
When nights are freezing and days are warmer

title: Penicillin: a lucky mistake
text: In September 1928, a Scottish doctor named Alexander Fleming came back to his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London after a summer holiday. He was not known for being tidy. On a shelf he found a dish in which he had grown bacteria, and he noticed something odd: mould was growing on it, and around the mould the bacteria had disappeared. Fleming realised that the mould, which was a type of Penicillium, produced something that killed bacteria. He called it penicillin. He wrote about his discovery in 1929, but at the time it was hard to make the substance in enough amounts, and the idea did not become a medicine straight away. More than ten years later, a team at Oxford University led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain worked out how to purify it and tested it. During the Second World War, factories in Britain and the United States made it in large quantities, and it saved the lives of many wounded soldiers who would have died from infections. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Penicillin was the first widely used antibiotic. Antibiotics treat infections caused by bacteria, but they do not work against viruses such as the cold or flu. Doctors now ask patients to take them only when needed and to finish the full course, because bacteria can slowly learn to resist the medicine. Fleming himself warned about this problem in his speech in 1945.

questions.q: Where did Alexander Fleming work?
options: At St Mary's Hospital in London

title: The London Underground
text: London has the oldest underground railway in the world. The first section opened on 10 January 1863 and ran between Paddington and Farringdon. Trains at the time were pulled by steam engines, so the tunnels filled with smoke, and passengers sometimes came out with dirty faces. Electric trains began to replace them from the end of the nineteenth century. Londoners call the system 'the Tube', because the deep lines have round tunnels shaped like tubes. Today it has around 270 stations and eleven lines, each with its own name and colour, such as the red Central line, the blue Piccadilly line and the yellow Circle line. Millions of journeys are made every week. The Tube map is a design classic. In 1931 an engineer called Harry Beck, who worked for the Underground, drew a simple diagram with straight lines and equal gaps between stations. He knew that passengers do not need a geographic map when they are underground; they only need to know which lines connect. The diagram was a success, and many cities have copied the style since. You will hear a famous recorded phrase at many stations: 'Mind the gap'. It warns passengers about the space between the train and the platform. Another rule is 'stand on the right' on escalators, so that people in a hurry can walk on the left. Some stations are also surprisingly beautiful, with tiles, murals and art. In the Underground, the world's first and best-known maps and signs live together under the busy streets.

Why is the Underground called 'the Tube'?
options: Deep lines have round, tube-shaped tunnels
It is shaped like a letter T

questions.q: What does 'Mind the gap' warn about?
options: The space between train and platform

title: The octopus: three hearts and clever arms
text: The octopus is one of the most remarkable animals in the sea. It has no bones, so it can squeeze through any hole bigger than its beak, which is the only hard part of its body. Stories about octopuses escaping from aquariums at night are told by workers all over the world, and some of them are true. Here is a surprising fact: an octopus has three hearts. Two of them pump blood through the gills, and the third sends blood around the rest of the body. Its blood is blue, because it uses a copper-based substance to carry oxygen, while human blood uses iron and is red. The octopus also has an unusual nervous system. Most of its neurons, the cells used for thinking and moving, are in its eight arms rather than in its head. Each arm can taste and touch, and can react quickly on its own. Scientists have seen octopuses open jars, solve puzzles and even use tools such as coconut shells as shelter. Octopuses are famous for camouflage. Special cells in their skin let them change colour and even texture within a second, so they can look like rocks, sand or seaweed. If a predator comes close, an octopus may shoot out a cloud of dark ink and swim away fast by squirting water from its body. Sadly, most octopuses live for only a few years. Some species live just one year or two. Even so, they use that short life to explore, hide and learn.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
Why is an octopus's blood blue?
options: It uses a copper-based substance to carry oxygen

title: Burns Night in Scotland
text: On 25 January, many people in Scotland and around the world hold a special dinner called a Burns Supper. It is a celebration of the life and poetry of Robert Burns, the national poet of Scotland, who was born on that date in 1759. Burns wrote many poems and songs in the Scots language, and his best-known work today is probably 'Auld Lang Syne', which millions of people sing at the end of New Year parties. The menu is traditional. The main dish is haggis, a savoury food made from sheep's heart, liver and lungs, minced with oats, onions and spices. It is served with 'neeps and tatties', which are mashed swede and mashed potato. Some people are surprised by the ingredients, but many say that haggis is delicious and a little peppery. There is a ceremony too. Often a bagpiper plays while the haggis is carried into the room. Then someone recites Burns's poem 'Address to a Haggis', which praises the dish in a very funny way, and cuts the haggis open with a knife. Guests also read other poems, tell stories and sing songs. At the end, everyone joins hands and sings 'Auld Lang Syne'. The evening is warm and playful. Many schools in Scotland also take part, so children learn some Scots words, such as 'wee' for little and 'bonnie' for pretty. Burns Night shows how a country can honour its writers by turning poetry into a party.

title: The Wright brothers' first flight
text: On the morning of 17 December 1903, on a windy beach near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, two brothers from Ohio made history. Orville and Wilbur Wright had built a machine with a wooden frame, cloth wings and a small petrol engine. They called it the Wright Flyer. That day, it became the first powered aircraft to carry a person in controlled flight. The brothers were not famous engineers. They ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and they learned by experiment. They built kites and gliders, and they made a small wind tunnel to test the shape of wings. They also understood that a pilot needed a way to control the aircraft, so they designed a system that twisted the wing tips slightly to turn and balance the machine. Orville flew the first flight. It lasted only 12 seconds and covered about 37 metres, which is less than the length of a Boeing 747. That day the brothers made four flights. The longest, by Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered 260 metres or so. A few minutes later, the wind knocked the aircraft over and damaged it, and it never flew again. Only a few people saw the first flights, and newspapers did not report them widely. The brothers continued to improve their designs, and by 1905 they could fly for more than half an hour. Within a few years, aeroplanes were being built in many countries. The original Wright Flyer is now in the Smithsonian museum in Washington, D.C.

How long was the first flight?
Where is the original Wright Flyer today?

In the Smithsonian museum in Washington, D.C.

title: Uluru: the red heart of Australia
text: In the middle of Australia, far from any big city, a huge red rock rises from the flat desert. This is Uluru, also known in the past as Ayers Rock. It is about 348 metres high, which is taller than the Eiffel Tower without its antenna, and it is around nine kilometres around the base. Most of the rock is actually underground. Uluru is made of sandstone, and its colour seems to change during the day. At sunrise and sunset it glows deep orange and red, and after rain it can look silver-grey with waterfalls pouring down its sides. Many visitors wake up early to watch the sun rise over the rock. The land is sacred to the Anangu, the traditional owners, who have lived in the area for tens of thousands of years. They tell stories, called Tjukurpa, about ancestors who created the landscape. Caves and rock paintings show that people have been there for a very long time. In 1985 the Australian government handed the land back to the Anangu, who lease it to the national park. Together they manage the park. For many years tourists climbed to the top, but the Anangu asked visitors not to, both out of respect and for safety. The climb was finally closed in October 2019. Instead, tourists can walk around the base, join a guided tour with an Anangu guide, or learn about bush food and tools. UNESCO has listed the park as a World Heritage Site for both its nature and culture.

Who are the traditional owners?
When was the climb closed?

title: Fish and chips
text: Fish and chips is one of the best-known meals in Britain. It is a piece of battered fish, usually cod or haddock, served with thick fried potatoes called chips. People often add salt and vinegar, and sometimes mushy peas, which are crushed green peas, or a spoonful of tartare sauce. The dish is really a mix of two traditions. Fried fish was brought to Britain by Jewish immigrants from Spain and Portugal, who had a way of frying fish in a crispy coating. Fried potatoes were popular in the north of England. Around the 1860s, shops began selling the two together. One early shop was opened in London by Joseph Malin, and another in Mossley, in Lancashire, by John Lees. Both are often named as the first. For many workers the dish was cheap and filling. Fish and chips became so important that they were not rationed during the Second World War, because the government felt that the meal helped to keep spirits high. By the 1930s, there were tens of thousands of chip shops across the country. In the past, the food was wrapped in old newspaper. This is no longer allowed for health reasons, but some shops use paper that looks like newspaper as a joke. Many people eat the meal outside by the sea, where seagulls are watching closely. If you visit a seaside town, hold your chips tightly: the birds are quick and bold.

What are mushy peas?

questions.q: Why were fish and chips not rationed in the war?
options: The government thought they kept spirits high

title: The Olympic Games, then and now
text: The first Olympic Games took place in ancient Greece, in a place called Olympia. Records say the earliest ones were held in 776 BC, and they took place every four years for more than a thousand years. At that time there were only men's events, and the main sports included running, wrestling and chariot racing. Athletes competed in the sun, and the winner received a crown made of olive leaves, not a gold medal. The Games ended around the end of the fourth century AD and were forgotten for a long time. In the nineteenth century, a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin wanted to bring them back to build friendship between nations through sport. The first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896. Fourteen nations took part, and there were about 240 athletes, all of them men. Women first competed in 1900 in Paris, in events such as tennis and golf. Winter Games were added in 1924. The Olympic flag has five rings, which represent the five inhabited continents joined together, and at least one of its colours appears in the flag of every country. One event has a particular history: the marathon. It was created for the 1896 Games to remember the story of a messenger running from the town of Marathon to Athens. The exact distance of 42.195 kilometres was fixed after the 1908 Games in London. Today the Olympics are held every four years, with Summer and Winter Games alternating every two years.

Who helped bring the Olympics back in modern times?
In which city were the first modern Games held?

title: Why is the sky blue?
text: It is a question that children ask, and scientists have an answer. Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mix of all the colours of the rainbow. You can see this when sunlight passes through a glass prism or through drops of rain. The air around the Earth is full of tiny molecules, mainly nitrogen and oxygen. When sunlight enters the atmosphere, these molecules scatter the light in all directions. The important point is that short wavelengths, such as blue, are scattered much more than long wavelengths, such as red. This process is called Rayleigh scattering, after the British physicist Lord Rayleigh, who explained it in the 1870s. As a result, blue light bounces around the whole sky, and when you look up, blue light reaches your eyes from every direction. You may ask: if violet has an even shorter wavelength, why is the sky not violet? There are several reasons. The Sun gives off less violet light than blue, some of the violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. The mix looks blue to us. At sunrise and sunset, the Sun is low, so its light has to pass through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue is scattered away on the long journey, and the remaining light is orange and red. That is why sunsets are so colourful. On the Moon, which has no atmosphere, the sky always looks black, even in the daytime.

questions.q: What is sunlight made of?
Why are sunsets red or orange?
options: The sky is painted by clouds
The light travels through more air and the blue is scattered away

title: The floating islands of Lake Titicaca
text: Lake Titicaca lies high in the Andes, on the border between Peru and Bolivia, at about 3,800 metres above sea level. It is often called the highest navigable lake in the world, meaning that large boats can sail on it. It is also one of the biggest lakes in South America, and on a sunny day its water is a deep, shining blue. On the Peruvian side, near the city of Puno, live the Uros, a people who have built artificial islands on the lake. The islands are made from totora, a tall reed that grows in the shallow water. The Uros cut blocks of the thick roots, tie them together, and then pile layers of dry reeds on top. The result is a soft, springy surface that you can walk on, though it feels a little like a mattress. Because the reeds at the bottom slowly rot in the water, the Uros must add fresh layers on top every few weeks. Their houses, boats and even some furniture are also made of totora. The reed is useful in other ways: people eat the soft white part of the stem, and they use the plant as a simple medicine for toothache. Many families once moved onto the islands for safety, and some now earn money by welcoming visitors. They sell woven crafts and give rides in boats shaped like animals. Not far away is Taquile Island, where men and women are known for beautiful knitting and weaving, which UNESCO recognised as part of the world's cultural heritage.

questions.q: What are the Uros islands made from?
Why must the Uros add new reeds on top?
options: The reeds at the bottom slowly rot
The reeds are eaten by birds

questions.q: Where is Lake Titicaca?
options: On the border of Peru and Bolivia

title: The Sydney Opera House
text: On the edge of Sydney Harbour, on a point of land called Bennelong Point, stands one of the most recognisable buildings of the twentieth century: the Sydney Opera House. Its roof looks like a group of white sails, or perhaps the shells of giant sea creatures, and it shines in the sun against the blue water. The design came from a competition in 1957. The winner was a Danish architect called Jørn Utzon, who was not very well known at the time. His idea was so original that no one knew exactly how to build it. Engineers spent years working out how to make the curved roof shells, and they finally found a solution by making all the shapes from parts of a single sphere, which allowed the pieces to be built in a factory. The project took much longer and cost much more than planned. It was expected to open in 1963 and cost about seven million Australian dollars, but it opened in 1973 and cost around 102 million. After a disagreement with the government, Utzon left Australia in 1966 and never saw the finished building. Queen Elizabeth II officially opened it on 20 October 1973. The roof is covered with more than one million tiles, which were made in Sweden. They are cream and white, and they are designed to clean themselves when it rains. Today the building holds concert halls, theatres and a studio, and it hosts about 1,500 performances every year. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage List in 2007, and every New Year's Eve fireworks light up the harbour behind it.

questions.q: Who designed the Opera House?
Why did the Opera House take so long?
options: It was a very difficult design to build
It was moved from another city

title: Ice hockey in Canada
text: For many Canadians, hockey is more than a sport. It is a part of national identity. Children learn to skate when they are very small, and in winter they play on frozen ponds and outdoor rinks. Families watch games together on Saturday nights, and a good hockey story can start a conversation with almost any Canadian. Ice hockey is played by two teams of six players, including a goalkeeper. They use sticks to hit a small hard rubber disc, called a puck, into the other team's net. The game is fast, and players change quickly during the match because skating at high speed is tiring. Historians say the first organised indoor game was played in Montreal on 3 March 1875, at the Victoria Skating Rink. The man who organised it, James Creighton, wrote rules based on field hockey and other games. At first the players used a flat piece of wood instead of a puck, and later they changed it to a rubber disc, because a ball could jump out of the rink and hit spectators. The most famous trophy is the Stanley Cup. It was donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, who was then the Governor General of Canada. Today it is awarded to the winner of the National Hockey League, and each player on the winning team is allowed to spend a short time with the trophy during the summer. Canada's national teams are among the best in the world, and fans were delighted when they won Olympic gold in men's hockey in 2002, 2010 and 2014.

title: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe
text: Every August, the Scottish capital turns into a giant stage. The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is the biggest arts festival in the world, with thousands of shows and many thousands of performers from all over the planet. There are comedians, actors, dancers, musicians and circus artists, and nearly any space can become a theatre. The Fringe began by accident in 1947. In that year, the first Edinburgh International Festival was organised to help bring people together after the Second World War. Only some performers were invited, but eight groups arrived without invitations and decided to perform anyway, on the 'fringe', or edge, of the official event. A journalist used the word in a newspaper, and the name stuck. Today you can watch a show in a theatre, a church hall, a café, a bus or a small tent. Some performances last an hour, and some are only a few minutes long. Entry prices vary: some shows are free and ask for donations at the end. The Royal Mile, the main street of the Old Town, becomes crowded with street performers handing out leaflets, juggling or dancing in costume to attract the audience. Many famous comedians and writers started their careers at the Fringe. For performers it is hard work, because there is a lot of competition, and the weather in Scotland can be wet. However, visitors love the atmosphere. At the same time, the city also hosts book, film and military band festivals, so August is one of the busiest months of the year.

How did the Fringe begin?
options: Eight groups performed without being invited
A company organised it for money

questions.q: What is the Royal Mile?
options: The main street of Edinburgh's Old Town

title: Tim Berners-Lee and the World Wide Web
text: Many people use the words 'internet' and 'web' as if they were the same thing, but they are different. The internet is the huge network of computers connected together around the world. The World Wide Web is a system for sharing pages and information on that network, and it was invented by a British computer scientist named Tim Berners-Lee. In 1989, Berners-Lee was working at CERN, the European research centre for particle physics, near Geneva in Switzerland. Scientists there came from many countries and used many different computers, so it was hard to find and share documents. He wrote a proposal describing a system in which documents could be linked together and read by anyone. His manager wrote a short comment on it: 'Vague but exciting'. Berners-Lee created the basic ideas that we still use today: HTML, a language for writing web pages, URLs, which are addresses for pages, and HTTP, a set of rules for sending pages to a browser. The first website went online at CERN in 1991, and it explained what the web was and how to use it. An important decision was made in 1993. CERN announced that the technology would be free for everyone to use, without any payment. This decision helped the web to grow incredibly quickly. Berners-Lee has said many times that the web should be open to all, and he has campaigned for people's privacy and for fair access. He was knighted in 2004 and now Sir Tim continues to work on making the web safer and more useful.

questions.q: What is the World Wide Web?
options: A system for sharing pages on the internet

questions.q: Where was Berners-Lee working in 1989?
options: At a bank in New York

questions.q: What happened in 1993?
options: The first mobile phone was sold
CERN made the technology free to use

title: Emperor penguins and the Antarctic winter
text: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest continent on Earth, and few animals can live there all year. One of them is the emperor penguin, the largest of all penguins. An adult can be more than one metre tall and weigh up to about forty kilograms. It cannot fly, but it is an excellent swimmer, and it can dive hundreds of metres deep to catch fish and squid. The life of an emperor penguin is extraordinary. In March or April, at the start of the Antarctic winter, penguins walk many kilometres across the ice to their breeding places. The female lays a single egg, then carefully passes it to the male and goes back to the sea to feed. She has not eaten for weeks. The father keeps the egg warm by balancing it on his feet and covering it with a fold of warm skin. He stays like this for around two months in temperatures that can fall below minus forty degrees Celsius, and he eats nothing during that time. To survive, the males huddle together in large groups. The penguins slowly move, so that each bird takes a turn in the warm middle and then goes to the cold edge. When the chick hatches, the mother returns with food in her stomach and feeds it. Then the parents take turns going to sea to bring more fish. By the end of the year, when the ice begins to break up, the young penguin is old enough to enter the water. Scientists worry because melting sea ice may cause problems for the colonies.

title: The Statue of Liberty
text: On a small island in New York Harbor, a giant green lady holds a torch up towards the sky. The Statue of Liberty has been welcoming ships to the United States for more than a century. For millions of immigrants who arrived by boat, it was the first sight of their new country. The statue was a gift from the people of France to the people of the United States, to celebrate friendship and the idea of freedom. It was designed by the French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi. The metal framework inside, which holds up the copper skin, was designed by Gustave Eiffel, the engineer who later built the Eiffel Tower in Paris. The statue was built in France, then taken apart and packed into more than 200 crates, and shipped across the Atlantic Ocean in 1885. It was rebuilt on its pedestal, and the opening ceremony took place on 28 October 1886. With its base, the monument is about 93 metres tall. The crown has seven rays, and you can climb up to it, although there are a lot of steps. In the left hand, the lady holds a tablet with the date of the American Declaration of Independence. The statue is made of thin copper sheets. Copper is a reddish-brown metal, but when it meets air and rain for many years, it slowly turns green. The statue first looked like a shiny new penny, and after about thirty years it had become the green colour that we know today. In 1984 UNESCO added the statue to the World Heritage List.

What made the statue turn green?
options: Copper reacting with air and rain for many years

title: Rugby: the game with a legend
text: Rugby is a team sport played with an oval ball, and it is one of the most popular games in Britain, Ireland, France, New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and Argentina. Players can carry, kick and pass the ball, but the ball must be passed backwards or sideways, not forwards. The aim is to score a try by touching the ball down over the opponents' line. The game gets its name from Rugby School, in the town of Rugby in England. According to a famous story, in 1823 a pupil named William Webb Ellis got tired of the rules of football, picked up the ball and ran with it. The story is celebrated in a plaque at the school. However, many historians think the tale was invented later, and they say that the game developed slowly as different schools changed their own rules. Whatever the truth, rugby spread quickly. In 1871, the Rugby Football Union was founded in London, and the first international match, between Scotland and England, was played that same year. Today there are two main forms, rugby union with fifteen players and rugby league with thirteen, and a shorter version, sevens, which has been an Olympic sport since 2016. The Rugby World Cup began in 1987, and the winner receives the Webb Ellis Cup. New Zealand, South Africa and England have each won the tournament, and South Africa has won more times than any other country. The Six Nations tournament in February and March, between England, France, Ireland, Italy, Scotland and Wales, is one of the biggest sporting events in Europe.

title: Wimbledon: strawberries, grass and tradition
text: Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world. It started in 1877 at a club in south-west London, and it takes place every year over two weeks in late June and early July. Of the four big tennis tournaments, called the Grand Slams, it is the only one still played on grass. The tournament is famous for its traditions. Players must wear almost entirely white clothing, a rule which dates from the nineteenth century, when white was thought to hide sweat marks. The rule is strict, and even the colour of a small logo is checked. The Royal Box, a special seating area on Centre Court, is where guests such as members of the royal family sometimes sit. The classic snack is strawberries and cream. Every year, the club sells a very large amount of strawberries to the crowd, picked fresh from farms in Kent, and each portion has about ten berries. Tea and ice cream are also popular with the crowd. Some people are happier to watch matches on a big screen on a hill outside the courts. Rain often stops play, and for many years the players waited in the changing rooms. In 2009 a sliding roof was added to Centre Court so that matches could continue, and later another was built over Court One. The singles champions receive a golden trophy and are invited to a special dinner the next day.

title: Chocolate: from bitter drink to sweet bar
text: Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows in warm, rainy places near the equator. The first people to use it were in Central and South America thousands of years ago, and recent studies suggest that cacao was used in the upper Amazon region long before it was used in Mexico. Later, the Maya and the Aztecs made a bitter drink from ground cacao seeds, mixed with water, chilli or spices. It was served cold and frothy, and the seeds were so valuable that they were sometimes used as money. Spanish explorers took cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century. Europeans found the bitter drink too strong, so they began to add sugar and warm it, and it became a fashionable luxury for rich families. For a long time chocolate was a drink and not a food that people could bite. This changed in the nineteenth century. In 1847 a British company, Fry's, made the first solid chocolate bar, using cocoa butter. Then in 1875, a Swiss chocolate maker named Daniel Peter added powdered milk made by his neighbour Henri Nestlé, and he created milk chocolate. In Britain, Cadbury launched its Dairy Milk bar in 1905. Today most cacao is grown in West Africa, especially in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, and small farmers harvest the large pods by hand. Peru also grows high-quality cacao, and its chocolate has won international prizes. Remember that one bar of chocolate comes from many pods, so it takes a lot of work to make this treat. Many shoppers now look for labels that show that farmers receive a fair price.

questions.q: Where does chocolate come from?
options: The leaves of a coffee plant
The roots of a sugar plant
The seeds of the cacao tree

options: A bitter drink from ground cacao

title: One small step: the Moon landing
text: On 16 July 1969, a huge rocket called Saturn V lifted off from Florida carrying three astronauts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. They were the crew of Apollo 11, and their mission was to land humans on the Moon for the first time. The journey to the Moon took about three days. When the spacecraft arrived, Collins stayed in orbit in the command module, called Columbia. Armstrong and Aldrin climbed into the lunar module, named Eagle, and began the descent. The landing was tense. The computer gave alarms, and the planned landing area was covered with rocks, so Armstrong flew the craft by hand to find a safe place. They landed on 20 July with very little fuel left. 'The Eagle has landed,' Armstrong said. A few hours later, Armstrong climbed down the ladder and put his boot on the surface. He said, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' Aldrin joined him soon afterwards. They walked and hopped in the low gravity, took photos, planted an American flag and collected about 21 kilograms of Moon rocks and soil to bring back to Earth. The walk lasted around two and a half hours. An estimated 600 million people around the world watched the event on television. On 24 July the crew splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean. In total, twelve people have walked on the Moon, all of them between 1969 and 1972. A plaque left on the Moon says that the astronauts came in peace for all mankind.

title: Hadrian's Wall
text: In the north of England there is a line of old stone that crosses the country from coast to coast. This is Hadrian's Wall, which was built by the Romans almost 1,900 years ago. Construction began in AD 122, when the Emperor Hadrian visited Britain and ordered a barrier to be built to mark the northern border of the Roman Empire. The wall is about 117 kilometres long, which is 73 modern miles or 80 Roman miles, and it runs from near Newcastle in the east to the Solway Firth in the west. Soldiers, not slaves, did most of the work, and it took around six years. It had forts, small gateways called milecastles every Roman mile, and watchtowers between them. Some parts were about four to five metres high. It was not only for defence. Soldiers used the gates to check people and goods that crossed, so it also worked a bit like a border post. Life on the wall was hard for the soldiers, who came from many parts of the empire, including what are now Belgium, Spain and Syria. At the fort of Vindolanda, archaeologists have found hundreds of thin wooden writing tablets with ink messages. They include a letter in which a woman named Claudia Severa invites her friend to her birthday party, which is one of the oldest known examples of writing by a woman in Latin. Others mention socks, beer and a request for warm underwear. In 1987 the wall became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today you can walk along the Hadrian's Wall Path, a trail of about 135 kilometres, and see the stones in the green hills.

options: To mark and guard the northern border of the Roman Empire

questions.q: What did archaeologists find at Vindolanda?
options: Wooden writing tablets with ink messages

title: Bats: the only flying mammals
text: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Other animals, such as flying squirrels, only glide through the air. A bat's wing is formed by thin skin stretched over very long finger bones, which is why the scientific name for the group means 'hand wing'. There are over 1,400 species of bat, and they make up around one fifth of all kinds of mammals. Many people think bats are blind, but this is a myth. All bats can see, and some see well. However, many species also use a clever system called echolocation to find their way and catch food in the dark. A bat makes high-pitched sounds, which are too high for most humans to hear. The sounds hit objects and return as echoes, and the bat's brain uses these echoes to build a picture of its surroundings. It can find an insect smaller than a coin in the dark. Bats are very useful. Many species eat insects, and a colony can eat huge numbers in a single night, which helps farmers by protecting crops. Others drink nectar from flowers and carry pollen from plant to plant. In tropical forests they also spread the seeds of fruit trees. Some of the plants we enjoy, including types of bananas and mangoes, depend partly on bats. Bats sleep during the day, often hanging upside down in caves, trees or old buildings. Hanging is easy for them because their feet grip without effort. Because bats live a long time but have few babies, they are sensitive to habitat loss, so many countries protect their roosts.

questions.q: What is special about bats?
options: They are the only mammals that truly fly

questions.q: How does echolocation work?
options: The bat listens to echoes of its own sounds
The bat sees in the dark using a light
The bat smells with its wings

questions.q: How do bats help people?
options: They eat insects and spread pollen and seeds

title: Mount Everest
text: Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level on Earth. It lies in the Himalayas, on the border between Nepal and Tibet, which is part of China. In 2020, Nepal and China announced its official height as 8,848.86 metres, usually rounded to 8,849. In Nepal it is called Sagarmatha, and in Tibetan it is Chomolungma. The English name comes from Sir George Everest, a British surveyor who was in charge of mapping India in the nineteenth century. In 1865 the mountain was named after him, although he himself had never seen it and had suggested that local names should be used. Many people tried to climb Everest in the first half of the twentieth century. On 29 May 1953, a New Zealand beekeeper, Edmund Hillary, and a Sherpa climber, Tenzing Norgay, became the first people confirmed to reach the top. They were part of a large British expedition led by John Hunt. The news arrived in London on the day of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation. Climbing Everest is extremely difficult. The air at the top contains about one third of the oxygen at sea level, so most climbers carry bottled oxygen. The temperature can be far below zero, the wind can be strong, and storms can arrive quickly. The Sherpa people, who live in the Himalayas, play an essential role. They fix ropes, carry equipment and guide climbers, and many are expert mountaineers themselves. Since 1953, thousands of people have reached the summit. Today there is also concern about waste left on the mountain, and teams now collect rubbish and bring it down.

Who were the first confirmed climbers to the top?
Why do most climbers use bottled oxygen?

title: The Grand Canyon
text: In the state of Arizona, the ground suddenly opens into one of the greatest views on Earth: the Grand Canyon. It is about 446 kilometres long, up to 29 kilometres wide and more than 1.6 kilometres deep. It is so big that it is hard for the eye to understand, and many visitors stand silent when they first see it. The canyon was cut by the Colorado River. Over millions of years, the river wore away the rock, carrying sand and stones downstream. Scientists believe that the river began carving the present canyon around five to six million years ago. Rain, ice and wind also helped to widen it. The colours of the walls come from different layers of rock, red, orange, pink and brown, and each layer tells a story about the past. At the bottom, the rocks are almost two billion years old. The Grand Canyon has been home to people for thousands of years. Several Native American groups, including the Havasupai, Hualapai and Navajo, have lived in or near it, and some still do today. In 1919 the area became a national park, and it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1979. Today about five million people visit every year. You can walk the trails, ride a mule, float down the river on a raft or look at the view from a viewing platform. Hikers are warned to bring plenty of water, because walking down is easy but climbing back up in the heat is very tiring. The weather at the top can be much cooler than at the bottom.

Why do hikers need to bring plenty of water?

There are no rivers in the area
The canyon is in a rainforest

title: Where do English words come from?
text: English has hundreds of thousands of words, and that is one reason why learning it can feel difficult. The answer to why there are so many lies in history. English began as a Germanic language, brought to Britain about 1,500 years ago by tribes called the Angles, Saxons and Jutes. Basic words such as house, water, mother, eat and sleep come from that time. Then other peoples arrived. The Vikings settled in the north and east, and they gave us words such as sky, egg, window and they. In 1066, the Normans from France conquered England, and for many years French was the language of the royal court. As a result, English has two words for many things. The animals in the field kept their old names, such as cow, sheep and pig, but the meat on the table took French names: beef, mutton and pork. English also borrowed from Latin and Greek, especially for science and learning. In later centuries, as British traders and explorers travelled around the world, they picked up words from other languages. 'Pyjamas' and 'shampoo' come from Hindi and Urdu, 'safari' from Swahili, 'ketchup' from a Chinese dialect, and 'chocolate' from a language of the Aztecs. 'Llama' came to English through Spanish from Quechua, the language of the Andes. The language keeps growing. Each year dictionaries add new words, many of them from technology and from different cultures. English is very good at borrowing, which means that when you learn English you also learn a little about the whole world.

title: Coffee: from Ethiopia to the world
text: Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world, and its story starts in the highlands of Ethiopia. A famous legend tells of a goat herder named Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became lively after eating red berries from a certain bush. Nobody can prove the story, but we know that coffee plants grew wild in Ethiopia, and that people began to drink coffee in the Arabian Peninsula, in what is now Yemen, by the fifteenth century. A coffee 'bean' is really the seed inside a small red fruit called a cherry. After the cherries are picked, the seeds are dried, cleaned and roasted. Roasting makes them brown and creates the smell that people love. Traders carried coffee to Turkey and then to Europe in the seventeenth century. The first coffee houses in England opened in Oxford in 1650 and in London in 1652. They were popular meeting places where men talked about news, business and science for the price of a penny, so they were nicknamed 'penny universities'. Some famous companies, including an insurance market called Lloyd's, began in coffee houses. Today coffee is grown in a belt of warm countries around the equator. Brazil is the world's largest producer, followed by Vietnam and Colombia. Peru is also an important exporter, and its coffee grows in high, green valleys such as Chanchamayo and Cajamarca; much of it is grown by small farmers and sold with fair-trade labels. Every year, people drink billions of cups, and many cultures have their own style, from Italian espresso to Turkish coffee.

title: Leap years: why February sometimes has 29 days
text: Most years have 365 days, but every four years we add an extra day, 29 February. This is called a leap year. Why do we need it? The answer is in space. The Earth takes about 365.2422 days to travel once around the Sun. If the calendar used only 365 days, it would slowly fall behind the seasons, and after a few hundred years summer would arrive in the middle of what the calendar says is spring. The ancient Romans had a confusing calendar, and in 45 BC, Julius Caesar introduced a new one with an extra day every four years. This was a good solution, but it was slightly too long, because 365.25 is a bit more than 365.2422. Over centuries, the difference grew to about ten days. In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII introduced a new calendar, the Gregorian calendar, which is still used in most countries today. Britain and its colonies did not change until 1752, and when they did, the day after 2 September was 14 September. The Gregorian calendar has a smart rule: a year is a leap year if it is divisible by four, except for century years, which must also be divisible by 400. So 1900 was not a leap year, but 2000 was. The next leap years are 2028 and 2032. People born on 29 February are sometimes called 'leaplings'. They may celebrate their birthday on 28 February or 1 March in normal years. There are about five million leaplings in the world, and in some towns they organise special parties just for them.

questions.q: Why do we have leap years?
options: The Earth takes slightly more than 365 days to orbit the Sun

title: The Amazon rainforest
text: The Amazon rainforest is the largest tropical rainforest in the world. Together with the Amazon River basin, it covers an area of about six to seven million square kilometres, and it spreads across nine countries. Brazil has the biggest share, about sixty per cent, and Peru is second with around thirteen per cent. The other countries include Colombia, Bolivia and Ecuador. The Amazon River is the largest river in the world by the volume of water it carries. It pours about a fifth of all the river water that flows into the oceans. During the rainy season, parts of the forest are flooded, and fish swim between the trees. The Amazon is full of life. Scientists estimate that it is home to about ten per cent of all known species. Jaguars, sloths, giant river otters, macaws and pink river dolphins live there, as well as millions of insects. New species are discovered all the time. In Peru, the Manu National Park is one of the places with the greatest variety of life on the planet, and the city of Iquitos is the largest city in the world that cannot be reached by road. People get there by plane or by boat along the river. The forest also helps the planet. Its trees store large amounts of carbon and release water vapour that forms clouds and rain. Many indigenous peoples have lived there for thousands of years, using plants for food and medicine. Today, farming, mining and illegal logging are cutting down parts of the forest, so projects led by local communities are trying to protect it for future generations.

title: Basketball: invented with peach baskets
text: Unlike most sports, basketball has a clear starting point. It was invented in December 1891 by James Naismith, a Canadian teacher, at a training school in Springfield, Massachusetts. His boss asked him to create a new indoor game for the students during the cold winter, because they were bored with exercises and could not play outside. Naismith had to find a game that was active but not too rough. He decided that players should throw a ball into a high target, so that nobody could simply run through the defenders. He nailed two peach baskets to the balconies of the gym, about three metres above the floor, and wrote thirteen simple rules. The first players used a football. Because the baskets still had bottoms, someone had to climb a ladder to take the ball out after each basket. Soon, someone cut out the bottom of the basket, and later metal hoops with nets were introduced. At first, teams had nine players. Today, five players per team play on the court. The game spread quickly to schools and colleges across North America. Women began playing within a year, and basketball was added to the Olympics for men in 1936 and for women in 1976. The NBA, the main professional league in the United States, began in 1949 after two earlier leagues joined together. Today basketball is played in nearly every country. Its popularity is helped by its simplicity: all you need is a ball and a hoop. Naismith himself is remembered with the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame, in Springfield.

title: Alexander Graham Bell and the telephone
text: Alexander Graham Bell was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1847. His family had always been interested in speech and sound: his father taught people how to speak clearly, and Bell's mother and, later, his wife were deaf. Bell himself became a teacher of deaf students. This work gave him a deep interest in how sound travels, and it led him to his greatest invention. In 1870, the family moved to Canada and then Bell went to Boston in the United States. There he worked with an assistant, Thomas Watson, to build a machine that could carry the human voice through a wire. The idea was to change sound waves into changing electric current, and then change them back into sound at the other end. Bell received a patent on 7 March 1876. A few days later, on 10 March, the first successful message was sent. According to Bell's notebook, he spoke into the machine in one room: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.' Watson heard it clearly in the next room. It was a very simple sentence, but it was an enormous step for communication. At first, many people did not see the use of a telephone. Soon, though, the idea took off, and the Bell Telephone Company was founded in 1877. Bell wanted people to greet each other with 'Ahoy!', a call used by sailors, but Thomas Edison's suggestion of 'Hello' became the norm. Later, Bell kept inventing, from kites and boats to a metal detector. He died in 1922, and during his funeral telephones across North America were silent for a minute.

title: The Northern Lights
text: On clear, dark winter nights in places such as northern Norway, Iceland, Finland, Canada and Alaska, the sky can suddenly fill with moving ribbons of green, pink and purple light. These are the Northern Lights, or aurora borealis. They are among the most beautiful natural shows on Earth, and thousands of tourists travel north every year hoping to see them. Where does the light come from? The Sun constantly sends out a stream of tiny charged particles, called the solar wind. When this wind reaches Earth, the planet's magnetic field guides many of the particles towards the north and south poles. There they crash into gases in the atmosphere, and the collisions release energy as light. It is similar to the way a neon sign glows when electricity passes through gas. The colour depends on the gas and the height. Oxygen about 100 kilometres up produces the common green light. Higher oxygen can give red. Nitrogen can create blue or purple at the edges. The lights can look like curtains, spirals or glowing arcs, and they often move slowly. In the 1600s, the scientist Galileo gave the lights their name: Aurora was the Roman goddess of the dawn, and Boreas was the Greek god of the north wind. The same phenomenon at the South Pole is called aurora australis, and it is visible from Antarctica and sometimes from Tasmania and New Zealand. To see the aurora, you need dark skies far from city lights, a clear night and a bit of patience. Forecasts of solar activity can help to predict a good night.

options: Particles from the Sun hitting gases in the atmosphere

title: Aussie slang: a language of shortcuts
text: Australian English has its own character, and one of its most famous features is slang. Australians love to shorten words and add a friendly ending, usually '-ie' or '-o'. This habit makes conversation sound relaxed and a little playful, and it often confuses visitors for the first few days. For example, 'breakfast' becomes 'brekkie', 'afternoon' becomes 'arvo', and a 'barbecue' is a 'barbie'. A 'service station' where you buy petrol is a 'servo', and a 'utility vehicle', similar to a pickup truck, is a 'ute'. Someone who studies at a university might be a 'uni student'. People say 'heaps' to mean 'a lot' ('Thanks heaps!') and 'no worries' to mean 'you're welcome' or 'don't worry about it'. A 'thong' in Australia is not underwear but a flip-flop sandal, which can lead to funny misunderstandings abroad. Some phrases are descriptive. If something is 'fair dinkum', it is genuine or true. If you are 'running late', you might say you will be there 'in a tick'. A friend may be called a 'mate', and the word is used for men and women alike. You may even hear a sentence like 'I'm going to the servo to get some brekkie for the barbie this arvo', and it is perfectly normal. The slang does not mean that Australians speak a different language. Most can switch easily to a neutral style at work or at school. Nevertheless, using a few of these words shows friendliness. If you visit Australia, try a cheerful 'G'day, mate!' and see how people smile.

title: Mary Anning, the fossil hunter
text: On the south coast of England, in the town of Lyme Regis, the cliffs are full of fossils. This part of the coast, now known as the Jurassic Coast, was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. It is the home of one of the most remarkable scientists of the nineteenth century: Mary Anning. Mary was born in 1799 into a poor family. Her father was a carpenter who also collected fossils and sold them to visitors, and Mary and her brother Joseph helped him after school. After her father died, the family had little money, so fossil hunting became more important. In about 1811, Joseph found the skull of a strange creature, and during the next year Mary dug out the rest of the skeleton. It was an ichthyosaur, a giant sea reptile that lived millions of years ago. It was one of the first to be found and studied properly. Later, Mary found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur in 1823, with a very long neck and small head, and part of a flying reptile called a pterosaur. She also realised that certain stones found inside fossils, called coprolites, were fossil poo, which gave scientists clues about the animals' diets. She became an expert, but because she was a woman from a working-class family, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London, and men often took credit for her findings. Only after her death in 1847 did the society recognise her. Today the Natural History Museum in London honours her, and children in Lyme Regis still search the beach for fossils.

title: Hogmanay: New Year in Scotland
text: In Scotland, the New Year is celebrated with such enthusiasm that it has its own name: Hogmanay. For many Scots it is a more important celebration than Christmas, and in the past it was the biggest winter festival of the year. Nobody is completely sure where the word comes from, and some experts think it might have French or Old Norse origins. The biggest party takes place in Edinburgh. Tens of thousands of people fill the streets in the city centre to watch music and fireworks launched from the castle. A torchlight procession is held the evening before. At midnight, everyone joins hands and sings 'Auld Lang Syne', a song based on a poem by Robert Burns. There are also customs in the home. One is 'first-footing': the first person to step through your door after midnight brings luck for the year. Traditionally, the best first-footer is a tall, dark-haired man. He brings small gifts, such as a piece of coal for a warm house, shortbread or black bun for food, and a coin for money. Families clean their homes before midnight so that they can start the new year fresh and tidy. On 1 January, some brave people jump into cold water in an event called the Loony Dook, held in South Queensferry near Edinburgh. They often wear fancy dress and run into the freezing River Forth for a few seconds. The chill is part of the fun, and the crowd cheers them on from the shore. Wherever you are in Scotland, the message is simple: welcome the new year with friends and a good song.

title: Niagara Falls
text: On the border between Canada and the United States, the Niagara River drops over a cliff in a roaring cloud of mist. Niagara Falls is made up of three waterfalls: Horseshoe Falls, which is mostly on the Canadian side, and the American Falls and the small Bridal Veil Falls on the American side. Horseshoe Falls is about 57 metres high, and millions of litres of water pour over every second. The sound can be heard from far away. The falls were created at the end of the last Ice Age, about 12,000 years ago, when melting glaciers sent water flowing between two of the Great Lakes, Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. Since then the falls have moved slowly upstream, because the water wears away the soft rock under the hard cap at the top. In the past, they moved about a metre a year, but today engineers control the erosion and the speed is much slower. Niagara has always attracted daring people. In 1859, a French acrobat called Charles Blondin crossed the gorge on a tightrope, and he did it several times, once carrying a person on his back. Tourists have been taking boat rides to the base of the falls since 1846 on a boat called the Maid of the Mist. Today visitors wear plastic raincoats and still get wet. The falls are also used to make electricity. Large power stations take some of the water before it falls, mostly at night and in winter, when fewer tourists are watching. This arrangement is regulated by a treaty between the two countries, so the falls remain beautiful during the day.

title: The haka: a Maori tradition
text: Before an international rugby match, the New Zealand team, the All Blacks, stand in a line, bend their knees, slap their bodies and shout in unison. They are performing the haka, a traditional dance of the Maori, the first people of New Zealand. The performance is powerful and moving, with strong stamping feet, fierce faces and loud voices. Many opponents wait respectfully, and the crowd usually goes quiet. Haka is not only for war, as many people think. It is a general word for dance or performance, and there are many kinds. Maori perform haka to welcome guests, to celebrate a happy event, to mark a sad occasion such as a funeral or to tell a story about their ancestors. Songs and movements express the pride of a group and its connection to its land and history. The haka used by the All Blacks for more than a century is called 'Ka Mate'. It is said to have been composed around 1820 by a chief named Te Rauparaha, who wrote it after he escaped from his enemies by hiding in a pit. It describes the moment he returned to the light and felt alive again. In 2005 the team introduced a new haka, 'Kapa o Pango', written for them. Women's teams, such as the Black Ferns, perform haka too. Haka is taught in schools, and groups compete in kapa haka festivals, which combine singing, dancing and storytelling. In 2024, a young member of the New Zealand Parliament performed a haka in the debating chamber, which made news around the world. For the Maori, haka is a living part of their culture, and showing respect when you watch it is important.
